courses.title: C++ Foundations — Levels 1–5
courses.summary: 52 lessons on the first language you can actually run: what C++ is and how source becomes an executable, output with cout and cerr and input with cin and getline, formatting, variables and the lifetime of one, const and constexpr, every built-in type, the whole operator set, implicit promotion and the four casts, if and switch, the loops, functions from declaration through overloading to recursion and callbacks, one- and multi-dimensional arrays, C-strings and std::string, then memory: addresses, object size and layout, pointers and pointer arithmetic, new and delete, and the bugs that follow them — dangling pointers, use after free, leaks, double deletion and buffer overruns.

courses.title: C++ Intermediate — Levels 6–8
courses.summary: 31 lessons on the parts that make C++ object-oriented: references from aliasing through forwarding references, classes and encapsulation with invariants that hold, constructors from default to delegating and the order they run in, destructors and RAII, this and method chaining, inheritance from public through virtual and the diamond, overriding and object slicing, abstract classes and polymorphic deletion, friends, and the operator set — arithmetic, comparison, assignment, streams, call, subscript, arrow and conversion.

courses.title: C++ Templates — Levels 9
courses.summary: 8 lessons on templates: why they exist at all, function templates and how a type is deduced, class templates that behave, non-type parameters, full and partial specialisation, variadic packs, and constraining a template so a wrong type is refused with a sentence instead of a page of errors.

courses.title: C++ Advanced — Levels 10–12
courses.summary: 26 lessons on the standard library, move semantics and exceptions: iterators as the contract, algorithms instead of hand-written loops, lambdas and comparators, containers and what each costs — including forward_list, unordered_multiset, unordered_multimap and the container adapters — then rvalue references and std::move, move constructors, the rule of five, RAII and shared ownership, copy elision, what an exception is, catching correctly, the three guarantees, copy and swap, and the exception tree with a noexcept whose answer depends on the type.

courses.title: C++ Testing and Structure — Levels 13–15
courses.summary: 24 lessons on testing, streams and files, and splitting a program across headers and sources: a test as an argument you can re-run, assert and static_assert, a tiny test harness, edge cases as the real test, reading a compiler error and a crash, and a debugging routine; then streams as stateful pipes, reading text properly, formatting, writing and reading files safely, stringstream, and parsing a data file; then declarations against definitions, the header and its source, namespaces, compiling and linking, static and inline, a build script, CMake in one page, and a project you can grow.

courses.title: C++ Algorithms and Concurrency — Levels 16–18
courses.summary: 26 lessons on data structures, concurrency and performance: measuring cost by counting, a linked list by hand and the doubly linked list that walks both ways, stacks, queues, binary search, a sort written by hand, how a hash table finds in one step, a binary tree, and choosing a structure; then threads and data races, lock_guard and the shape of a scope, deadlock and lock ordering, atomics, async and future, condition variables, when not to use threads, recursive_mutex, packaged_task; then performance by measurement — cache locality, the cost of an allocation, needless copies, algorithmic cost before micro-optimisation, profiling, what the optimiser may do, and a checklist.

courses.title: C++ Design and Mastery — Levels 19–20
courses.summary: 16 lessons on designing larger programs and then building one: separating the interface from the implementation, the factory, the strategy and the observer, dependency direction, errors across layers, testing a layered program and a worked design; then chrono, filesystem, random, the algorithms worth knowing and type erasure as a generic boundary; then a three-lesson capstone that reads a requirement, gives it a structure, and tests and reviews the result.

courses.title: C++ Revision — Language Core and Library Gaps
courses.summary: 28 revision lessons closing the gaps between Levels 9 and 20: type aliases, enum class with its underlying type, decltype and decltype(auto), structured bindings, value categories in one lesson, alignment and padding, std::byte and endianness, bit masks, flags, bitset and bit fields, iterator categories and invalidation, the copy, fill, replace, rotate, sort, search and numeric algorithms people skip, variant, any, optional, string_view and span, pair and tuple, std::function and reference_wrapper, the testing frameworks, fixtures and parameterised tests, property-based and fuzz testing by hand, the preprocessor and its pitfalls, writing an algorithm for any iterator, test doubles, and where all of it sits in the roadmap.

courses.title: C++ Revision — Data Structures, Algorithms and Memory
courses.summary: 25 revision lessons on the structures and algorithms the levels build on: dynamic arrays and linked lists by hand, stacks, queues and a ring buffer, binary search trees, AVL rotations, what red-black trees guarantee, heaps and priority_queue, a binary heap by hand, tries, graph representations, breadth- and depth-first search with cycle detection, Dijkstra, topological sort, union-find, hash tables and collision handling, Big O and what it does not tell you, recursion and backtracking, memoisation and tabulation, merge and quick sort by hand, counting and radix sort, allocators and std::pmr, perfect forwarding, and a thread pool with the three ways to stall.

courses.title: C++ Memory Model and Object Lifetime — Levels 21–23
courses.summary: 16 lessons on what the standard actually promises: objects, storage duration and lifetime, happens-before and synchronizes-with, relaxed ordering, acquire and release, sequential consistency and why volatile is not atomic; what undefined behaviour means, the common sources one by one, and how to detect them before your users do; then the segments — text, data, BSS, stack and heap — stack frames and the direction of growth, static storage and initialisation order, sizing a class up, construction and destruction order, temporaries and lifetime extension, storage reuse with placement new, and what ends a lifetime in a union.

courses.title: C++ Preprocessor, Modules and Namespaces — Levels 24–26
courses.summary: 24 lessons on the preprocessor, modules and namespaces: the preprocessor as a text pass and not the compiler, #include with angles and quotes, #define and why constexpr wins, conditional compilation, feature flags, header guards and #pragma once, function-like macros and their traps, #, ##, __VA_ARGS__ and __VA_OPT__; then why modules exist, the shape of a module, what you export, implementation units and partitions, import, export import and the global module fragment, compiling one for real, headers against modules and a small modular project; then namespaces — nested, aliased, anonymous, inline — using declarations and their risks, and argument-dependent lookup.

courses.title: C++ Advanced STL, Ranges and Utilities — Levels 27–29
courses.summary: 25 lessons on the containers and utilities that finish the standard library: size, capacity and what a vector costs, iterator invalidation, erase-remove and the C++20 one-liner, choosing a container by complexity rather than habit, map and the operator[] trap, set against unordered set, std::array, and measuring instead of believing; then ranges and views — concepts, laziness, transform, take, drop, split, and pipelines where order matters; then variant and visit, optional with monadic chaining, any and its cost, string_view, span, std::expected, and pooling resources against a monotonic one.

courses.title: C++ Time, Randomness, Regex and Debugging — Levels 30–32
courses.summary: 24 lessons on the parts of C++ that touch the real world: chrono durations, clocks, time points, the calendar, weekdays, time zones and why an offset is not a zone, and formatting a date; then random engines as a sequence you can replay, distributions instead of modulo, and seeding the device once; then std::regex from regex_match and regex_search through capture groups, regex_replace and sregex_iterator, and when not to use a regex at all; then debugging — assert against throwing, reading a call stack, stepping, breakpoints and watch expressions, hunting leaks and use-after-free, the sanitizers, and the debuggers themselves.

courses.title: C++ Build Systems, Linking and Architecture — Levels 33–35
courses.summary: 26 lessons on how a program is made and how it is structured: the four stages behind one compiler command, reading a diagnostic, optimisation levels, defines, Make as a graph, Ninja and incremental builds, CMake with targets, libraries, install rules and tests, and MSBuild's properties, items and targets; then linking — symbols, declarations against definitions, the one definition rule, static and shared libraries, reading a link error, linking an external library, and choosing between the two kinds; then design — SOLID, DRY, KISS and YAGNI as decisions, factories and builders, adapters and decorators, command, state, visitor, template method, prototype and singleton, MVC, components and plugins, and abstract factory.

courses.title: C++ Testing, Performance and Threads — Levels 36–38
courses.summary: 24 lessons on proving a program works and making it fast: what a test is, unit, integration and system tests, test doubles that replace the clock and the disk, what a test framework does behind its macros, fixtures and fresh state, table-driven boundary tests, and how to make code testable at all; then performance engineering by measurement — optimisation levels, counting calls and counting work, reading a profiler, counting allocations, cache lines and traversal order, data layout, branches and vectorisation; then threads — the shared-memory rule, locks and the size of a critical section, thread pools and work queues, condition variables, atomics and memory order, lock-free progress, parallel algorithms, false sharing and the limits of scaling.

courses.title: C++ Networking, Databases and GUIs — Levels 39–41
courses.summary: 25 lessons on taking a program outside its own process: addresses and byte order, a server in five calls, UDP and what a stream actually promises, what a web request really is, names and DNS, one thread per client and where that stops, reading a message out of a stream, and choosing a protocol; then databases — what one holds, why values never become code, both-or-neither, the N+1 problem, connection pooling, indexes as a second sorted copy, one fact in one place and choosing an engine; then GUIs from the event loop outwards — a button that calls your function, computed layout, model and view, logic out of the widgets, long work off the loop, widgets against immediate mode, what a screenshot cannot show, and Qt, GTK and MFC compared side by side.

courses.title: C++ Games, Embedded Systems and Operating Systems — Levels 42-44
courses.summary: 25 lessons taking C++ out of the ordinary program: games as a loop and a sixteen-millisecond frame, input as a queue, velocity and acceleration, collision and reflection, entities and components, and a position becoming light on a screen, with SDL, SFML, OpenGL, Vulkan, DirectX and Unreal compared by how much of the frame each one owns; then embedded — a register and its datasheet, interrupts, running on time rather than fast, fixed point, flash against RAM, scheduling without an operating system, no heap and no surprises, and the half you can test on a desk; then operating systems — four jobs behind one privileged boundary, a process as a kernel record, scheduling, page tables, syscalls, pipes and shared memory, and where a bug is not just a bug.

courses.title: C++ Linux, Windows and Security — Levels 45-47
courses.summary: 25 lessons on the two systems C++ is mostly written for, and on making the result hard to break: eight on Linux — file descriptors, fork's two returns, exec, pipes as bytes rather than messages, signals and the short list a handler may do, mmap, a file in your address space, choosing the unit of isolation, and a shell in forty lines; eight on Windows — handles as indices, reference counts and inheritance, the registry, services, Winsock, UTF-16 inside and UTF-8 outside, COM as a vtable with a reference count, and an abstraction that names its leaks; and nine on security — threat arithmetic, length as the vulnerability, integer overflow, secrets that leak through copies, integrity rather than secrecy, timing, seeding, hardening, and the four rules of secure memory. Every mechanism runs as portable C++; the POSIX and Win32 calls it stands for are shown beside it.

courses.title: C++ Templates, Compilers and the Standard — Levels 48–50
courses.summary: 25 lessons on the machinery under the language: advanced templates from instantiation and two-phase lookup through SFINAE and concepts, parameter packs, CRTP, policies and compile-time work to reading a real error — and asking the compiler a question about a type with void_t and the detection idiom; then a compiler built card by card — lexer, recursive-descent parser with precedence, an AST you can walk three ways, three-address IR, optimisation passes that are counted, code generation for a stack machine, and the ABI of calling conventions, layout and name mangling; then the standard itself — how a paper becomes a feature, the release train to C++26, feature-test macros, deprecation, ABI stability, code that keeps compiling, and testing the machine instead of the year.

courses.title: C++ Professional Practice, Expert Techniques and Coroutines — Levels 51–53
courses.summary: 24 lessons on the work that separates a programmer who can write C++ from one a team depends on: professional practice, from a history a reviewer can read and a CI pipeline that gates rather than decorates to warnings as errors, sanitizers, a small linter, coverage and the honest number; expert technique — pimpl and ABI stability, lookup you can use on purpose, pointer provenance, expression templates, and a small executor; and coroutines from the frame outwards — a hand-written promise_type, co_yield and co_return, custom awaitables, the object behind the coroutine, counting and removing allocations, lazy pipelines, cancellation, and a standard generator rather than a hand-rolled one.

courses.title: C++ Library Design and Real Projects — Levels 54–55
courses.summary: 16 lessons on designing and shipping a C++ library and then building six real programs: header-only against static and shared, the header the consumer sees, what a consumer actually compiled, two versions in one binary, find_package, the layout a consumer cannot see, the translation unit everyone compiles, and a tag on a commit CI has proven; then a calculator, a ring-buffer logger, a thread pool, a binary file format that refuses the damaged file, a command-line tool a script can use, and a test harness — each small enough to read whole.

courses.title: C++ Projects — Build Them End to End
courses.summary: 12 lessons, six projects, every one built from nothing and run: a vector on raw memory with three pointers, placement new, growth counted move by move, and the strong guarantee kept when a copy throws; a string that owns its bytes with all five special members, and copy-on-write with the defect that ended it; unique_ptr written by hand as a move-only type, and shared_ptr with a real control block, atomic counts and weak references; an HTTP server answering three requests over one loopback connection, its parser refusing malformed input and naming the rule it broke; a log analyser reading 20,000 lines in one pass with no per-line allocation, and top-N with a min-heap; and a pipeline of stages with bounded queues, its backpressure measured — 94,841 refusals and 5,000 stage activations become 7,488 and 625 with batching. Every number in the prose was printed by the card beside it.

courses.title: HTML — Level 1 Preview: HTML and the Browser (3 Lessons)
courses.summary: Feedback preview with the first three Level 1 lessons: HTML structure and meaning; the distinct roles of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; and the path from source to a browser-rendered page. The rest of Levels 1–3 is still in production; this is not the complete Part 1 course.
